ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn (ferry terminal) / ⚓ Landeyjahöfn
en: This harbour has no bay, no headland and no natural shelter. It was built on an open black beach that the sea has been trying to fill in ever since.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn (ferry terminal) / ⚓ Landeyjahöfn
en: Before **2010** these islands were three hours from anywhere. The ferry ran out of **Þorlákshöfn** — about **2 hours 45 minutes** on the water, and a drive at the far end on top of that. Landeyjahöfn cut the crossing to about **35 minutes** and took Reykjavík to Heimaey from about four hours down to two. The first ship came in on **20 July 2010**, scheduled service the next morning. For **4,518 islanders** that is not a convenience. **That is the difference between living offshore and living up the road.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn (ferry terminal) / ⚓ Landeyjahöfn
en: The catch is that they built it on a beach that moves. No bay, no headland, nothing to hide behind — black sand and the open North Atlantic. Roughly **400,000 cubic metres of sand a year** travels east past this spot, most of it handed over by the **Markarfljót**, the glacial river you crossed on the way here. The glacier grinds the rock, the river carries it down, and the sea posts it straight through the harbour mouth. So a dredger has to dig it back out — and the dredger needs **five calm days in a row**, which an Icelandic winter does not hand out. (Ask nicely all you like.) **This harbour is downstream of a glacier, and the glacier does not negotiate.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn (ferry terminal) / ⚓ Landeyjahöfn
en: When it shuts, the ship does not stop — it simply goes to **Þorlákshöfn** instead, which turns a **35-minute** hop into **2 hours 45 minutes** on the water plus a drive at both ends, and on the worst days it does not sail at all. Every hospital appointment in Reykjavík, every lorry of fresh fish, every away match and every funeral gets re-planned around a wave forecast. **Ask an islander about this harbour and you will not get a neutral answer.**

en: The Island That Was Born on Television

ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey
en: Out there is an island younger than the Beatles. Nobody is allowed to set foot on it, and that is precisely the point.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey
en: It started **18 km south-west of the island we're heading for**. Early on the morning of **14 November 1963** the sea out there began to smoke — the eruption had been climbing through **about 130 metres of water** for days before anybody noticed — and by **15 November**, one day later, there was an island. It did not stop until **5 June 1967**: **three and a half years**, one of the longest eruptions in Iceland's recorded history — and the longest unbroken one. They named it for **Surtur**, the fire giant who rides up from the south at the end of the world with a burning sword. (Understated, the Norse.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey
en: It has been shrinking every day since the fire went out. Surtsey came out of the sea at about **2.7 km²** and stood **171 metres** high. By **2006** the waves had chewed it back to roughly **1.4 km²** — close to half of it gone in forty years. The loose ash and tuff goes first, now at something like **a hectare a year**, and underneath sits a hard basalt core. The arithmetic says that in **another 160 years or so** the core is all that will be left. **You are looking at an island with an expiry date.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey
en: Iceland worked out what it had before the eruption had even finished. Umhverfisstofnun's own phrase for the place is *náttúruleg rannsóknarstofa* — **a natural laboratory.** The word for what they are watching is *landnám*, **colonisation** — the very same word Icelanders use for the settlement of Iceland itself. Sterile rock, day zero, and every arrival since logged *án áhrifa mannsins*, **without the influence of man.** That record has now run unbroken for **more than sixty years.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey
en: They locked it in **1965**, while it was still erupting — not afterwards, during. The stated reason was to stop people importing life on a boot sole: *til að forðast aðflutning lífvera af mannavöldum*, **to avoid the arrival of organisms by human agency.** The reserve was widened to **65 km²** in **2006**, taking in the whole volcano and the sea around it, and **UNESCO listed it in 2008.** Landing needs a permit. **You are not getting one, and neither am I.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey
en: The first colonist was too small to see. Diatoms were found on the new rock in **August 1964**, nine months in. The first insect turned up even earlier, in **May 1964** — the volcano was still going. The first flowering plant waited until **1965**: *fjörukál*, **sea rocket**, arriving the only way anything arrives out there, as a seed on the current. Sea first, then wind, then birds. **The order of arrival is not a guess here. It is a logbook.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey
en: Then, in **1970**, something nested. Three years after the fire went out, researchers found *tvö hreiður teistu og eitt fýlshreiður* — **two black guillemot nests and one fulmar nest.** Three nests, on an entire island. **Thirteen bird species** have bred there since, and this is the turn in the story: a bird is not a visitor. **A bird is a delivery service**, carrying seed in its gut and fertiliser in its rear.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🌋 Surtsey
en: The gulls did the rest, and they did it with droppings. In **1986** the lesser black-backed gull, *sílamáfur*, bred on Surtsey for the first time; by **1990** there were close to **200 breeding pairs.** Vísindavefurinn is blunt about what followed — the gull has had by far the greatest effect on the island's vegetation, both by spreading seed and *ekki síður með driti sínu*, **no less by its droppings.** Vascular plants went from **21 species in 1985 to 43 by 1995**, and **60 by 2003**, plus roughly **300 species of small invertebrate.** **A colony of gulls built the soil, and the soil built everything else.**

ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur
en: We are sailing into this harbour through a gap between a cliff that is 40,000 years old and a lava wall that did not exist when your parents were born.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur
en: The cliff on your right is older than everything else you will see today. That is **Heimaklettur**, **279 metres**, the tallest of the **Norðurklettar**, the North Rocks. It is **móberg of around 40,000 years** — the ash-and-rubble stone you get when a volcano erupts under ice or under the sea and the water quenches the lava before it can flow. Its northern summit, **Hákollar**, tops out at **283 metres** and is **the highest point in the whole archipelago.** The town below it is the newcomer.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur
en: **Dufþaksskor** — the ledge named for Dufþakur, the ringleader from the story I gave you on the mainland — is on the side you cannot see from here, on the **north face**, turned away from the harbour and out towards the open sea. Note carefully: it is local scholarship that fixes the spot, **not *Landnámabók***, so take it as tradition rather than gospel. But it is very precise tradition. **The islanders know exactly which crack in the rock they mean.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur
en: Beside it runs **Dufþekja**, the green slope — *ákaflega flá og brött*, **extremely sloping and steep** — and men fell off it with grim regularity. The belief was that **twenty people had to perish there before it would be finished**, the same number as in **Jökulsá á Sólheimasandi**, the glacial river out on the black sand of the south coast. The two places were said to *kallast á* about their dead, **to call to one another.** Dufþakur was counted the first. **The final tally is put at twenty-one or twenty-two.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur
en: Nobody went up there for the view. Dufþekja was *mikið fýlapláss* — **a great fulmar place** — and before that a source of *hvönn*, angelica, and of roots dug out of the turf. Men climbed that face because a fulmar chick is dinner and angelica is medicine, and on an island with no forest and no fields there was no other way to get either. **Every single death on that slope was an economic decision that went wrong.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur
en: The names are written down, which is what stops this being folklore. **Jón Árnason** of Vilborgarstaðir, about **70**, fell on **24 August 1823.** **Jón Ólafsson** of Elínarhús, **28**, on **20 July 1825.** **Hannes Sæmundsson** of Nýibær, **26**, on **21 July 1858** while digging roots — and his body washed ashore at **Kross in Landeyjar**, on the flat mainland shore you sailed from. Then the last: **Ísleifur Jónsson** of Hlaðbær, about **20**, caught by falling rock in the **earthquake of 26 August 1896** and dead of his injuries on **31 August.** After that, they said, the slope was satisfied.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur
en: Now the wall on your left, which did not exist in 1972. That is **1973 lava** from **Eldfell.** Before the eruption this harbour lay open to the south-east and took a beating in every winter gale. The flow crept down, stopped **just short of sealing the entrance**, and left behind a breakwater no engineer could have got funded. The islanders lost **417 houses** and **gained one of the best harbours in the country.** Nobody here calls that a fair trade. **Nobody here denies the harbour is better, either.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🏔️ Heimaklettur
en: Both halves of the founding story are on one side of this rail. Off to your right is **Eið**, the low green neck where Ingólfur found the ten of them sitting down to a meal — and above the neck, on the **north face of Heimaklettur**, is **Dufþaksskor**, where the chase ended. The supper and the fall in a single look, without turning your head, **and about eleven and a half centuries sit between them and the concrete under your feet.**

ctx: the point of the block — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named
en: Icelanders named every grass ledge on that mountain because they grazed sheep on them. They never named the elephant, because nobody here had ever seen one.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named
en: The most photographed rock on this island has a name given to it by the internet and no name at all from the people who live under it.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named
en: Everyone on this boat has seen a photo of that rock. Almost everything written about it online is wrong, including its name.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named
en: Start with the name, because the name is wrong. The internet calls it **Elephant Rock** and hands you a confident Icelandic original: **Halldórsskora.** So go and look Halldórsskora up. It sits at entry **358** in the old Vestmannaeyjar place-name register, and the entry reads, in full: *“hér er grastó og lömbum beitt þar á vetrum”* — **here is a grassy ledge, and lambs were pastured there in winter.** Not a cliff. Not an elephant. **A different mountain altogether.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named
en: **What you are actually looking at has no Icelandic name at all.** It is part of the **Norðurklettar**, the oldest exposed rock on Heimaey at roughly **40,000 years** — the same subglacial **móberg** as Heimaklettur, ash and rubble welded together under ice or sea. And while we are correcting things: the widely repeated claim that this is **columnar basalt** is **not supported by any Icelandic geological source.** Móberg does not form columns. **It does exactly this — soft, layered, and carved by weather into a face.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named
en: **Eleven centuries, and nobody once thought elephant.** Islanders named the ledges, the clefts, the hollows, the bird-cliffs and every patch of winter grazing on these mountains, because they had to climb them and work them. They looked straight at that head and that trunk for a thousand years and saw **rock they could not graze.** **The elephant needed an outsider with a camera.** It is a shape you can only see if you have no job to do on it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named
en: The register is the joke in itself. It was compiled by **Gísli Lárusson**, and it is exhaustive to the point of comedy. Entry **358** is **Halldórsskora**, the grazing ledge. Entry **359** is **Halldórsskorukórar** — **the little grassy hollows next to Halldórsskora.** They named the ledge, and then they went back and named the dents beside the ledge. **Hundreds of entries, every one of them earned by somebody who had to climb it, cut it, graze it or fall off it.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named
en: And the mountain is the young part of this. Vísindavefurinn traces the **Vestmannaeyjar volcanic system back 70,000 to 100,000 years**, sitting on sea floor that is **ten million** years old, under **700 m** of marine sediment full of shell fossils. So: **Surtsey is from 1963. The elephant is 40,000. The floor beneath both of them is ten million.** Three orders of magnitude in one view, and only one of them has a name in English.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named
en: The elephant is a fashion, and fashions are dateable. Not one Icelandic source records the resemblance — no folk tale, no place name, no entry in Gísli Lárusson's register. It appears with the aerial photograph and the phone camera. **We can date almost every other name on this coastline to within a century. The most famous one we cannot date at all, because it has no history — only a feed.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Landeyjahöfn → Heimaey (the crossing) / 🐘 The Elephant Iceland Never Named
en: Practical note, so you do not spend the rest of the day hunting for it. **You will not get the face from this deck, and you will not get it from the road either.** It sits on the seaward side of **Ystiklettur**, turned away from the harbour, and from the land it is about **641 m across a ridge** — both further and rougher than that number sounds. That is exactly why **every photograph you know of that rock was taken from a boat.** It is not one angle among several. It is the only angle there is. If you want the shot, you want the sea, and that is a separate morning.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🏡 Herjólfsdalur
en: **Margrét Hermanns-Auðardóttir** put a trowel into this valley in **1971** and did not stop until **1980**, turning up **eight houses** across roughly **1,300 m².** Then she published a date and the room went cold. The oldest layers, she argued, sit *underneath* the **landnámslag** — the pale settlement ash of **871** that every archaeological trench in Iceland is measured against. If she is right, somebody was living in this bowl **before Ingólfur ever saw Reykjavík.** It is not accepted: **Orri Vésteinsson** calls the claim *“as yet lacking proper documentation and cannot be verified.”* But notice what nobody disputes — **the eight houses are real.** Only the date is heretical.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🏡 Herjólfsdalur
en: The turf farm in front of you went up in **October 2005**, a longhouse and an animal house rebuilt from the dig's own ground plans, and it is meant to be the farm of **Herjólfur Bárðarson.** And even *he* is contested. *Hauksbók* says *“Herjólfur Bárðarson, bróðir Hallgríms Sviðbálka, byggði fyrst Vestmannaeyjar”* — **Herjólfur built here first.** *Sturlubók* gives the credit to his son **Ormur.** The argument is not between the sagas and the archaeology. **It is inside one book, between two copies of it.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🏡 Herjólfsdalur
en: One letter is doing an enormous amount of work here. *Sturlubók* actually calls him *“Ormur ánauðgi, son Bárðar Bárekssonar”* — **Ormur the enslaved.** **Sigfús M. Johnsen** reads that as a scribe's slip for *auðgi*, **the wealthy**, and then reconciles the two manuscripts by letting both be true in sequence: **Herjólfur settled the valley, and his son Ormur inherited it**, farmed at **Ormsstaðir** and ended up owning **every island in the group.** One wobbling vowel is the difference between the richest man in the archipelago and somebody else's property.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🏡 Herjólfsdalur
en: Then a raven, a rockfall, and the daughter who walked out. Herjólfur had a daughter, **Vilborg**, and she is why this valley has a sequel. The crag of **Molda** came down on the farm — and the story says a bird got there first: *“sagði hrafn Vilborgu við skriðunni og bjargaði þannig lífi hennar”*, **a raven told Vilborg of the landslide and so saved her life.** The record tags it *“sögunni samkvæmt”*, **according to the story** — which is the polite Icelandic way of saying do not build a thesis on this.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur (the festival valley) / 🏡 Herjólfsdalur
en: She had already fallen out with him over water. Herjólfur, by the local account, **charged people to draw from his spring**, and Vilborg handed it out free in the evenings. (Iceland's first pricing dispute, settled by geology.) When the rockfall settled the argument she built her own farm at **Vilborgarstaðir**, beside a pool she named **Vilpa**, and laid down a rule — *“skyldi engum verða meint af vatni úr Vilpu”*, **no one was to be denied water from Vilpa**, however unlovely it looked. **Hold on to Vilborgarstaðir.** That is where the islanders held their assembly, and the ruling I will give you at the horse gully was made there.

en: It began on **Sunday 2 August 1874** — the thousandth anniversary of the settlement, and the year the Danish king finally handed Iceland a constitution. Districts the length of the country threw a millennium festival that summer, and then **everyone else let it lapse. ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Herjólfsdalur → Stórhöfði / 🐴 Kaplagjóta

So the assembly did the sums, set a hard ceiling, gave it teeth in the shape of the king's agent, and attached a **14-day** fuse. **This is a medieval community legislating its own carrying capacity — and enforcing it over a cliff.**

en: **Stórhöfði** is **122 m** high, the southernmost tip of Heimaey, thrown up in a **submarine eruption about 6,000 years ago** and then tethered to the rest of the island by a thin low neck called **Aur** — **Brimurð** on the east side of it, **Vík** and **Klauf** on the west. Stand on that neck and there is open Atlantic on both sides of you at once. The **lighthouse went up in 1906**, and the wind set about it immediately. ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði
en: **17 September 1921, and it has not missed a day since.** The lighthouse keeper **Jónathan Jónsson** started taking readings alongside the lamp. **Three times a day at first** — kl. 8, 14 and 21 — then five or six a day **from 1922**, **seven from 1941**, and **eight since 1952**, at 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24. **Not a day missed in over a century.** The **annual mean wind speed is 11 m/s**, **13.2 in January** and **8 in July**, and wind has been clocked here at **130 knots, about 67 m/s.** In **2005** the **World Meteorological Organization** accredited the station to its strictest international standard, one of only three in Iceland alongside **Keflavík** and **Akureyri.** A century of unbroken data off a rock this exposed is a genuinely rare object.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði
en: **One family has been reading this weather for over a hundred years.** **Jónathan Jónsson** kept the light from **1910 to 1935.** His son **Sigurður V. Jónathansson** took it from **1935 until his death in 1966.** His son **Óskar J. Sigurðsson** held it from **1966 to 2007.** His son **Pálmi Freyr Sigurðsson** has it now. **Four generations, one headland, one unbroken record.** That is exactly why the data off this rock is worth so much — nobody moved house, so nothing was ever interrupted.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði
en: Be accurate if a guest pushes back: **Stórhöfði does not hold Iceland's wind records**, and that is the single most repeated error told about this place. **Skálafell** holds the ten-minute mean at **62.5 m/s**, set on **20 January 1998.** **Gagnheiði** holds the gust at **74.5 m/s**, set on **16 January 1995.** What Stórhöfði holds is not the peak. It is the **relentlessness** — a mean of **11 m/s** year in and year out, roughly **four genuinely calm days a year**, and **86 fog days**, more than anywhere else in the country. Anywhere in Iceland can have one appalling afternoon. This place has had a century of them.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði
en: What that wind actually does to things: windblown sand off the beaches scoured the lighthouse glass so badly that **the light itself became useless** — and the fix was not engineering but botany, planting sand grasses on the slopes below to hold the ground down. Waves of up to **30 m** have been measured off this headland. Annual rainfall runs about **1,556 mm** on the **1961–2000** mean, and most of it arrives sideways. (Umbrellas here are a spectator sport.) When somebody tells you Iceland has weather rather than climate, this is the address they have in mind.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði
en: **Óskar J. Sigurðsson** ringed seabirds off this headland from **1953 to 2014** — **91,695 individual birds** across some **40 species**, mostly puffins, then fulmars and snow buntings. By **1997** *Guinness World Records* had entered him as the person who had ringed more birds than anyone else on earth. He was not a scientist on a grant and he had no field station. He was the lighthouse keeper, and this is what he did between observations.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði
en: **This is the densest puffin ground in the archipelago.** Vestmannaeyjar as a whole holds **840,375 breeding pairs** — about **41.5% of every puffin in Iceland.** The burrows are packed into the grass slopes below you like a housing estate, which is more or less what they are. And the colony is in trouble: numbers have fallen by more than **3% a year since 1998**, and in **2018** the puffin went onto Iceland's Red List as **Critically Endangered.** Islanders hunted these birds for food for centuries. Now they count them instead, which is a harder job and pays worse.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Stórhöfði (the headland) / 🌬️ Stórhöfði
en: In late August the pufflings get it catastrophically wrong. The **pysjur** leave the burrows after dark and navigate towards the brightest thing on the horizon, which for several million years was the moon on the water and is now a fishing town with street lighting. They come down in gardens, in car parks, in the middle of the main street. Since **2003** the **Pysjueftirlitið** — the puffling patrol — has organised the island's children to go out at night with cardboard boxes, collect them, **weigh them, measure a wing**, and then carry them to the cliff edge and throw them at the sea. About **a quarter are ringed** on the way past. **This is a town where primary-school children do seabird fieldwork as an evening activity, and think nothing of it.**

en: **Eldfell did not exist on the evening of 22 January 1973.** Every stone under your boots arrived in the small hours that followed, which puts this mountain's birthday inside living memory. **For thirty-seven years this was the youngest mountain in Iceland — until Fimmvörðuháls in 2010.** It is still the youngest with a town at the foot of it. Published heights run anywhere from **200 to 220 m** — which is not sloppiness, it is the honest answer for a cone whose scree is still settling. The red colour is iron oxidising in the scoria. **The mountain is, quite literally, rusting.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell
en: **Nobody was warned.** Iceland had recorded **small earthquakes of around magnitude 3 in the two days before**, and their unusual depth pointed to magma rather than ordinary faulting — but no announcement was made. **A magnitude 3.0 struck at 01:40, and the fissure opened in the small hours that followed — the accounts differ by a few minutes and nobody has ever pinned it exactly.** Two islanders happened to be out walking near midnight and watched it happen: *«Jörðin hreinlega opnaðist og eldtungur skutust upp á yfirborðið»* — **the earth simply opened and tongues of fire shot up to the surface.** The fissure tore open **east of Kirkjubær**, one of the island's oldest farm sites, along the edge of the settled ground. **Evacuation began within thirty minutes.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell
en: **A 1,600-metre fissure with 30 to 40 vents**, and it opened along the eastern edge of a working fishing town of **5,273 people** — the count taken on **1 December 1972**, seven weeks before. It did not stop for **five and a half months**; the eruption was not declared over until **3 July 1973.** For the whole of that spring Heimaey was a disaster zone, a building site and an active volcano at the same time, and people went to work in it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell
en: The arithmetic of the damage, and the arithmetic of the gain. Out of **1,350 houses** on the island, **417 were buried outright** and roughly **400 more were damaged.** Meanwhile the island itself got bigger — **11.2 km² before, 13.44 km² after**, a gain of about **2.2 km²** from roughly **0.25 km³** of erupted material. The town lost around a third of its buildings and gained a fifth of its surface area. **Nobody here calls that a fair trade.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell
en: They fought the lava with the sea, and won. By **4 February** the flow was pouring into the harbour mouth with such force that the harbour was **closed to all traffic from 4 to 20 February.** The front was advancing about **200 m a day**, straight at the entrance channel — and the harbour is the reason the town exists. The physicist **Þorbjörn Sigurgeirsson**, who had watched Surtsey do much the same thing a decade earlier, proposed the only idea available: *«að stýra hrauninu með því að dæla á það sjó»* — **steer the lava by pumping sea water onto it.** For the dates I am leaning on the islands' own eruption chronicle, which is a community record rather than an institution, so take it as the islanders' own: **the cooling trials starting on 6 February, the dredger Hákur brought in on 13 March, and the American pumps landing on 28 March.** By **30 March** the volume was up by a further **50%.** The front chilled, crusted and turned aside. **The harbour survived.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell
en: And here is what pumping seawater onto lava actually does, because it is not what it sounds like. Þorbjörn's own figures, as translated in **USGS Open-File Report 97-724**: each cubic metre of water cools about **0.7 m³ of lava**, and a single stationary jet at **100 litres a second**, held on one spot for days, will chill about **a hectare** of flow. *“A solid layer of lava about 1 m thick will form in 24 hours.”* Boreholes drilled afterwards found the cooling had driven **13 to 15 metres down** after roughly two weeks of pumping. So you are not putting the eruption out and you are not freezing the flow. **You aren't cooling the lava — you're building a dam out of it, and the still-molten inside has to go round.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell
en: Nothing was wasted, which is very Icelandic. Before **1973** the island had a chronic shortage of fill material — you could not build anything here without tearing up somewhere else to get gravel. The eruption solved that overnight. The ash carted off the streets went, among other places, into **lengthening Heimaey's airport runway**, an extension Icelandic sources say would otherwise simply not have been possible. The new lava gave the town ground for housing, for sports pitches and for the road you came in on.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell
en: Then they sent the volcano a bill. It worked for roughly **ten years** before the heat faded, and then they went back to electricity. **Part of the cost of the eruption was paid, quite literally, by the eruption.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldfell (the 1973 cone) / 🌋 Eldfell
en: And then they had a row about what to call it. A hard south-easterly had blown all through the previous day and **only dropped at about ten o'clock that evening**, a few hours before the ground opened. On any ordinary January night those boats would have been out on the grounds, twenty miles away. Instead they were in the harbour, fuelled and crewed, and they carried **between 4,300 and 4,500 people** to the mainland in roughly **four hours.** Set that against a population of five thousand-odd and you are short by about **500** — and those went out **by air from the airfield through the morning**, which is the part the boat story always leaves out. One **300-tonne** boat, *Gjafar* **VE 300** under skipper **Rafn Kristjánsson**, took **430 people** in a single crossing — *«fólk var í borðsal, í göngum, klefum aftur í og fram í»*, **people were in the mess, in the passageways, in the cabins fore and aft.** **Not one person was hurt.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey
en: The clean-up was brutal arithmetic. Roughly **800,000 tonnes** of ash and pumice had to come off the streets and off the roofs, and the roofs were the urgent part — wet ash is heavy enough to bring down a house the lava never touched. Crews worked at it right through the spring and the summer. The moment the islanders themselves point to is **6 September 1973**, the day **the street lights came back on.** Not the harbour, not the fish plant, not the shop. The street lights — **because that is when a buried town starts to look like a town again after dark.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey
en: And then, without anybody ordering them to, they came back. There was no compulsion, no guarantee the mountain had finished, and no sensible reason to be first. **About 1,200 were home by mid-September 1973.** Over **2,000 by November.** They moved into a town that was still half-buried, still smelled of sulphur, and was still warm underfoot when you walked across the new ground. The eruption had been over for barely two months.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey
en: But not all of them, and this is the part worth saying plainly. **Hagstofa Íslands**, the national statistics office, counted **5,303** people here at the end of **1972.** At the end of **1973** it was **4,906.** At the end of **1974** it bottomed out at **4,396** — **907 fewer** than before the eruption. Half a century on, the island has still never got back to its **1972** figure. The town survived. **Around a sixth of the people who made it never came home, and every family here can name one of them.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey
en: Why they came back is tied up at the end of this street. This is the **only harbour on the entire south coast of Iceland** between **Þorlákshöfn** and **Höfn í Hornafirði** — everything in between is surf and black sand with nowhere to put a boat. That is why there is a town here at all, and it is why the fight to save the harbour mouth in February 1973 was a fight for the town's existence rather than its convenience. Today it runs **just under two kilometres of quay** — Siglingastofnun's figure is **1,978 m** — with an entrance dredged to **9.5 m.** The vessel count I would stand behind is a **2005** snapshot: **78 registered vessels** working out of **58 companies.** The islanders' own formulation is blunt — **the harbour is the precondition for settlement in the islands.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Heimaey town (lunch stop) / 🐟 Heimaey
en: And what you are having lunch in: an island of **4,518 people** (**1 January 2026**), a harbour the eruption accidentally improved, and a working fish town that happens to have a volcano at the end of the road. What strikes visitors is the complete absence of memorial solemnity. **1973** is not treated here as a tragedy to be observed. It is treated as a thing that happened, was dealt with, and has since been turned into a museum, a set of walking paths and a very good view.

ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar
en: The house you are standing in is **Gerðisbraut 10.** It belonged to **Gerður Sigurðardóttir** and **Guðni Ólafsson**, and they lived here with **three young children** — the youngest **only a few weeks old.** This was never a monument or a landmark or a site of any historical significance. It was a family's kitchen, a family's sitting room and a family's bedrooms, and on the night of **23 January 1973** they had minutes to decide what mattered.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar
en: **What they took with them was a bottle for the baby.** That is the entire inventory. In the dark, with the eastern sky lit up and the ground shaking under the floor, **Gerður** and **Guðni** walked out of this house carrying an infant, two other children and **a feeding bottle.** Nothing else. Everything around you now is what they left standing where it stood. They never lived here again. Nobody did. And roughly **five thousand** other people made a version of that same decision within about an hour of one another, almost all of them on the same assumption — **that they would be back in a week to collect the rest.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar
en: It stayed buried for **more than forty years.** Ash and pumice sealed the house where it stood, at the foot of the cone that produced them. The digging began in the summer of **2005** under the working name ***Pompei norðursins*** — **the Pompeii of the North.** When **Gerðisbraut 10** came back up, the decision was taken not to move it, not to restore it and not to tidy it. The museum was built **over the house, where the house is.** **You are standing inside the actual room.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar
en: And it was not the only house they dug out. The **Pompei norðursins** excavation went street by street through ground nobody had walked on since **1973.** **Suðurvegur 25** came up first. **Suðurvegur 16** was uncovered on **7 July 2006** and **Suðurvegur 18** on **25 July 2006**, and the work reached into **Búastaðabraut**, **Gerðisbraut** and the ground around **Helgafellsbraut.** These are real streets with real house numbers, and for more than four decades the only measurable thing about them was the depth of pumice on top.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar
en: One house, standing in for four hundred. **The museum's own text says almost 400 homes and businesses. The islands' eruption chronicle puts it at 417 buried outright.** Either way, **roughly a third of every building on Heimaey.** You cannot exhibit that. What you can do is excavate one entirely ordinary home, leave the crushed roof and the buckled walls exactly as the pumice left them, and let one family's rooms carry the weight of all the others. **That is the whole curatorial decision behind this building, and it is why people who came in expecting a geology museum tend to come out quiet.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar
en: **Eldheimar opened on 23 May 2014.** RÚV carried it that day under the headline *Gosminjasafnið Eldheimar opnað í Eyjum.* You will also see the museum's own phrase, **forty years after the eruption**, which rounds you back to 2013 — but that is a turn of speech, not a second opening date. **Inside a building whose whole purpose is to get one night exactly right, it is worth being exact about its own.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar
en: Upstairs is the other eruption. The **Surtsey exhibition** opened on **14 November 2014** — deliberately, the anniversary of the day in **1963** that Surtsey broke the surface. Two eruptions, one roof, and they mean opposite things to the people who live here. **Surtsey made new land where there had been none, and nobody lost anything. Eldfell made new land too, and it took 417 homes to do it.** The islanders live with both, and they do not confuse them.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Eldheimar (the eruption museum) / 🏚️ Eldheimar
en: Be straight with people about the death toll, because it is genuinely contested. **Icelandic institutional sources record no deaths from the eruption.** International volcanology — **the USGS** and **Oregon State** among them — records **one death, from volcanic gas** that pooled in a low-lying space. Those two accounts have never been reconciled, and I am not going to reconcile them for you on a Tuesday afternoon. What I will say is that the lurid version some guides tell, a looter overcome in a pharmacy basement, **is not documented in any source I would stand behind.** A town of **5,273** people evacuated from under an erupting fissure with, at the very most, one fatality. **That is the fact. It does not need decorating.**

ctx: opening hook line — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn
en: The islanders built a fort to stop pirates. In 1627 the pirates arrived, looked at it, and simply landed somewhere else.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn
en: Built for the wrong enemy, and then left to rot. **Kornhólsskans** — nobody calls it that, everyone says **Skansinn**, from the Danish *skanse*, a redoubt — went up in **1586** on the orders of the Danish crown, to protect the royal trade monopoly against **English privateers.** The king sent a naval officer, **Hans Holst**, with the men, the tools and the guns. The islanders were made to do the labour **unpaid**, and were given free provisions in lieu of wages. (A packed lunch, essentially.) By around **1600** the English threat had faded and Denmark stopped maintaining the place. **That decision is the hinge of everything that follows.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn
en: **16 July 1627.** Three ships out of **Algiers**, roughly **300 men.** They had already been working the Icelandic coast for a fortnight and had taken **110 captives between 5 and 13 July** before they ever reached here. They tried to put men ashore at **Kópavík** and found it too awkward, so they went round and landed at a spit that has been called **Ræningjatangi** — **Raiders' Point** — ever since. The fort had cannon and it had men with powder. It was also **unfinished and a generation neglected**, and the raiders simply declined to sail past it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn
en: The Danish trader here was **Lauritz Bagge**, and his last act before he ran is the good bit. He looked at three shiploads of armed men, did the arithmetic, and got his family into a rowing boat for the mainland — but not before making certain the raiders got nothing usable out of him. His captain went out to the trading ship, **bored holes in her hull and cut her moorings** so she would either drift ashore or go down. Bagge himself went to the guns: *«kaupmaður gekk svo frá fallbyssunum, að þær skyldu eigi nytjast ræningjunum, ef þær féllu í þeirra hendur»* — **the merchant left the cannon in such a state that they would be of no use to the raiders, if they fell into their hands.** He could not save the islanders. **He could at least deny the enemy the artillery.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn
en: They killed about **36 people** and carried off **242 islanders** to be **sold at auction in Algiers.** Around **200 got away by hiding** — in the fish-drying caves at **Fiskhellar**, in **Hundraðmannahellir**, the Cave of a Hundred Men above Herjólfsdalur, and behind **Sængurkonusteinn**, the Childbed Woman's Stone, where tradition holds a woman nursing an infant was found and, for once, spared. Add those three numbers and you have a community of barely **500 souls.** **242 of them gone in a single day is not a raid. It is the removal of a generation.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn
en: They sent one man back to ask for money. **Ólafur Egilsson** was the elderly priest of the islands. He was taken with the rest, then released in Algiers almost immediately for one specific purpose — **to travel to Denmark and Iceland and raise the ransom for everybody else.** He crossed Europe on foot and by ship and reached home on **6 July 1628**, not quite a year after he had been dragged off this shore, carrying the news of exactly who was still alive and what each of them was priced at. He also wrote it down. His ***Reisubók*** is one of the strangest documents in Icelandic literature — **a captivity narrative composed by the hostage who was sent home to fundraise for the other hostages.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn
en: The ransom took the better part of a decade. Money was collected across **Iceland, Denmark and Norway**, and in the end about **35 Icelanders** were bought back, roughly **27 of them islanders**, home after some **nine years.** Among them was **Guðríður Símonardóttir**, whom Iceland has never stopped calling **Tyrkja-Gudda.** In the autumn of **1636** the freed captives were held in **Copenhagen** to have their Lutheran faith refreshed before they were let home, and the student assigned to teach them was a young man called **Hallgrímur Pétursson.** She was about **sixteen years older** than he was. They came back to Iceland in the spring of **1637** and married. He went on to write the ***Passíusálmar***, printed at **Hólar in 1666** and reprinted **more than ninety times** since — the most read book of verse in the language. **It comes out of this beach.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn
en: Iceland's answer to 1627 was drill. The fort was rebuilt properly and Denmark sent **a military instructor** to run the defence of the islands, and **every able-bodied man** was required to turn out for weekly weapons practice. From **1639** the gunner at Skansinn was **Jón Ólafsson Indíafari** — 'the India-farer' — who had sailed for the Danish crown as far as India, come home injured, and now sat on a rock in the North Atlantic waiting for ships that never came back. **The raid never repeated. The drills carried on for generations anyway.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 8.0 / Skansinn (the harbour fort) / 🏰 Skansinn
en: Then **1973** rearranged the whole scene. The lava came through here as well and changed the ground, the shoreline and the view completely — what you are looking at is a reconstruction standing on the original site. And there is a great deal packed into about forty metres: **Landlyst**, just here, went up in **1847** and is among the oldest houses in Iceland, with Iceland's **first maternity hospital** built beside it in **1849**; the **water tank** dates from **1931**; and **Klemensarkirkja**, the Norwegian **stave church**, was given to Iceland by **Norway** for the thousandth anniversary of the conversion and consecrated on **30 July 2000**, presented by **King Harald.** **A fort, a maternity ward, a water tank and a Viking-age church, all standing on ground that is itself only fifty years old.**

Then Hamburg's **Hanseatic** men muscled in, and the two sides spent the best part of a century licensing, seizing and occasionally shooting at one another over dried fish, until the Danish crown lost patience and shut the lot behind a **royal trade monopoly in 1602.** (Iceland's first hostile takeover. ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Keflavíkurflugvöllur → Njarðvík / 🏘️ Keflavík

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Keflavíkurflugvöllur → Njarðvík / 🏘️ Keflavík

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌑 Route 41
en: Reading the age of it is easy once you know the trick: nothing grows on it. The jet-black, plant-free fields are the new ones. These older flows, **east of the new ones** toward Hafnarfjörður, are ~**700–1,000 years old** — medieval — and still look like last week's, because Iceland has almost **no weathering**: no acid rain, no baking heat, no forest to break the rock down. Cold, clean Atlantic air preserves lava almost perfectly. (Nothing tidies up here. It just sits there looking new for a thousand years, like a show home.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌑 Route 41
en: And a fair bit of it is hollow. **Lava tubes** form where the surface crusts over while molten rock keeps running underneath, then drains away and leaves the pipe behind. The whole pile is hundreds of metres thick — but the hollow tubes are just under the crust, sometimes only a metre or two below the wheels. (You are, in a modest way, driving on a ceiling.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires
en: The **Reykjanes Fires** are a recurring cycle: the peninsula sleeps for centuries, then wakes for decades of eruptions across several systems, then sleeps again. The last full cycle ran ~**950–1240 CE** and laid most of the lava we've driven on.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires
en: After **1240 it went quiet for ~800 years** — then on **19 March 2021** a fissure split open at **Fagradalsfjall** and the Fires restarted. That first show ran six months; **50,000+** people hiked out to watch a volcano like it was a gig.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires
en: Then **Meradalir (2022)** and **Litli-Hrútur** ("Little Ram", **2023**), before the action jumped north to the **Sundhnúkur crater row** by Grindavík: **nine eruptions there between December 2023 and August 2025** — **twelve on the peninsula since 2021.** The last ended **early August 2025.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires
en: As of **2026** there is **no active eruption** — the **longest pause yet** — but magma is still pooling under **Svartsengi**, and the Met Office (**Veðurstofan**) rates a fresh eruption the **most likely near-term outcome.** Their hazard map runs a six-level colour scale, green through yellow and orange to red, across zones **A to F.** Grindavík is zone A, and it currently sits at **yellow — *nokkur hætta*, some hazard.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires
en: That first eruption ran **six months to the day** — **19 March to 18 September 2021** — and left about **150 million cubic metres** of lava over **4.8 km²**, averaging **more than 30 metres thick**, peaking in May and June at around **12 cubic metres a second.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires
en: Under Svartsengi right now there is **about 28 million cubic metres** of magma on the Met Office's assessment — and that assessment runs out on **30 September**, which tells you how fast this moves. The ground is still rising at roughly **2 cm a month**, which makes today's quiet the pause between two eruptions rather than the end of anything.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires
en: **Could it go off while we're here?** Honestly — it could. There's about **twenty-eight million cubic metres** of magma under Svartsengi and the Met Office's own assessment says an eruption is the **most likely next event.** Here's the part that matters: when it moves, it moves **sideways first**, and that gives somewhere between **twenty minutes and four hours** of warning. Iceland has evacuated this ground **nine times** and has **not lost a single person to lava.** If it happens today, we'll know before it reaches the surface, and we'll be somewhere else.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires
en: Krýsuvík did the same job last time round. The **Krýsuvíkureldar of 1151 to 1188** laid down **Ögmundarhraun**, **Mávahlíðahraun** and **Kapelluhraun**, and then the system shut for **eight centuries** and has not opened since.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🔥 The Reykjanes Fires
en: **Kristján Sæmundsson** and **Magnús Á. Sigurgeirsson** call **Fagradalsfjall** unlike any other system on the peninsula — no central volcano, no proper fissure swarm, no high-temperature field, roughly **5 km wide and 15 km long.** Its **picrite** comes up fast and from deep without loitering in a chamber, which is why nothing filled up slowly where the instruments could watch it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌋 Grindavík
en: **Grindavík** was settled ~**934 CE** — one of the first Reykjanes communities and a major North Atlantic **cod harbour.** It even caught the **1627 Barbary corsair** raids. By December 2023 it held about **3,720 people.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌋 Grindavík
en: On **10 November 2023**, thousands of earthquakes in a few hours ripped **fissures metres wide** through roads, gardens and house foundations. The whole town was **evacuated in one night.** In **January 2024**, lava reached the streets for the first time — houses burned, roads buried.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌋 Grindavík
en: Further eruptions followed through 2024 and into 2025 as the **Sundhnúkur crater row** kept reactivating. **6 m earthen barriers** built in days saved some streets and were overrun on others. For all that, **none of this lava ever reached the sea** — it crossed the Grindavíkurvegur road again and again and pushed into the town on **14 January 2024**, but it never made the coast. The last time lava ran into the sea on this peninsula was the **12th century.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌋 Grindavík
en: And then people started coming back. The state buyout company **Þórkatla** bought **over 90% of the homes** and most residents did leave for good — but at **1 April 2026** Þjóðskrá had **874 registered residents** living in Grindavík again, against about **3,720** before the evacuation. The **school is open** for the autumn term, crews have worked all summer to get **Bókasafn Grindavíkur**, the town library, back on its feet, and the **harbour and the power plant never stopped at all.** In **April 2026** Alþingi debated a formal framework for rebuilding the community here. ctx: fact bullet — tour 12.0 / Njarðvík → Vogar / 🌋 Grindavík
